title: Bank ledger
like: the core ledger of a bank
brief: You run the system of record for a regional bank: every deposit, withdrawal and card settlement is a posting that must be exact and permanent. Customers in two continents read balances all day, and regulators can ask for proof at any time. A bad day for you is a loss of even one posting.

clarify.q: Can a posting ever be edited or deleted?
clarify.a: Never. Corrections are new postings. The ledger is append-only.

clarify.q: How much data can we lose in a disaster?
clarify.a: None for acknowledged postings. If a region is lost we may be down for minutes, but not wrong.
About 60 percent in North America and 40 percent in Europe.

clarify.q: What must we prove to the regulator?
clarify.a: An audit trail, encryption with managed keys, tested backups, signed-in access and long retention.

notes: A posting is one double-entry record: a debit and a credit.
Recovery time target: 15 minutes. Recovery point target: zero.

Scored data retention: at least 2555 days on active authoritative stores. Copies used only for search or reports can be rebuilt. Local device history and rollup policies still require the separate protocol check.

numbers.label: Balance reads per second at peak
Ledger rows written per day at 60 percent average load

hints: Which copy of the data is the truth during a failover? A write that only reached one copy can disappear.
Use a strict, immutable ledger with synchronous replication across zones. For a whole-region loss you need a second region, kept warm, plus backups you have tested.
The operation id and balanced entries must share the same transaction. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: A bank ledger is a lesson in what to refuse: no caches on balances, no async replication for acknowledged postings, no deleting. A strict immutable store replicates in step across zones, so a zone or a database failover loses nothing. A second region held ready, with tested backups, turns a region outage into minutes of downtime instead of a disaster. Corruption is answered by point-in-time restore from backups.

designs.name: Ledger shards with an active-active second region
designs.why: Purpose-built ledger shards with sync replication across 3 zones carry the money. A second region in Europe runs active-active: it takes over in about 30 seconds and loses nothing, and it costs about as much as the main region again. A warm standby would cost about 40 percent, but it takes about 15 minutes and can lose the last few seconds of postings, which breaks the zero-loss target. Backups give a clean restore point before any bad change. Sizing budget (approx.): 6,000 requests/s with one retry allows 12,000 attempts/s. At 1,000 requests/s per app server, that is 12 servers, or 18 with one of three zones reserved for failure. The measured fleet is sized for the peak and recovery day. These are total fleet counts, not counts per customer region. Both continents reach the US primary; EU reads pay the cross-region round trip. The active-active recovery plan mirrors the linked services in Europe at about twice the cost and takes over in about 30 seconds, rather than halving normal load between two drawn app fleets.

designs.name: Distributed SQL with an active second region
designs.why: Consensus keeps the authoritative data in agreement. An active second region protects every linked service; guarded releases prevent corrupt migrations. The traffic result still needs the checked ledger transaction rules.

tradeoffs: Sync replication across zones adds about 2 to 5 ms to every posting and is the price of never losing an acknowledged one.

Active-active costs about 100 percent of the primary region again and recovers in about 30 seconds with nothing lost. A warm standby costs about 40 percent and takes about 15 minutes; pilot light costs about 10 percent and takes about an hour. A zero recovery-point target leaves only active-active (approx.).
Not caching balances costs more database. A cached balance that is a few seconds old is a customer seeing money that is not there.
Backups are the only defence against a bad migration or a corrupting bug that every replica faithfully copies. Replication is not a backup.
EU customers pay about 80 ms per round trip to the primary region. That fits a 500 ms posting target and would not fit a 50 ms one.
editorial.realWorld: Retail banks run ledgers at hundreds to a few thousand postings a second and typically target a recovery point of zero and a recovery time of minutes to an hour (approx.).

correctness.prompt: What ledger invariant do you protect, and how do concurrent transfers and retries preserve it?
correctness.discussion: Every transfer has immutable entries whose debits equal credits, so money is conserved. Commit all entries, the unique transfer id and the saved result in one transaction. Lock balances in a consistent order or use serializable isolation with retries to prevent spending the same available funds twice. A retry returns the original result. A ledger component and synchronous replication alone do not prove these rules. Immutable debits equal credits is a per-commit invariant. Replication does not provide an atomic available-funds check. The operation id and balanced entries must share the same transaction.

fields.label: Step 1. Transfer T debits 20 and credits 19. May it commit?
options: Reject it because each transfer must balance
Commit now and fix the missing unit in reconciliation
fields.explanation: Immutable debits equal credits is a per-commit invariant.

fields.label: Step 2. Two withdrawals read the same available balance. What serializes spending?
options: Read from replicas and merge balances later
Lock balances in a stable order or use serializable transactions with retries
fields.explanation: Replication does not provide an atomic available-funds check.

fields.label: Step 3. T committed but its reply was lost. What does retry return?
options: A second posting followed by a compensating entry
The saved result under T committed with all entries
fields.explanation: The operation id and balanced entries must share the same transaction.

correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
correctness.responsibility: Commit balanced postings exactly once and prevent concurrent overspending.
